amendments.rule: **A subordinating conjunction the ASV supplies for a clause whose Hebrew writes none is `added`.** Casuistic law opens its protasis with אִם, with כִּי, or with a waw, and where one of these stands in the clause it takes the ASV's *if*, *when* or *that* by rules 14 and 30: the corpus aligns a waw to *if* and to *when*, and כִּי takes whichever of them the ASV has written for it. But the ASV also writes such a word for a clause that has no conjunction in it at all — *and, behold,* ***if*** *the plague be spread* for וְהִנֵּה פָּשָׂה הַנֶּגַע, and the italic ***yet*** of *he is bald,* ***yet*** *is he clean* for קֵרֵחַ הוּא טָהוֹר הוּא — and there no morpheme licenses it: it is its own `added` unit under rule 30. Do not fold it into the waw that opens the clause, into הִנֵּה, or into the verb, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also* — the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them, and the waw and הִנֵּה already have the *and* and the *behold* the ASV wrote for them. Count the clause's conjunctions against the ASV's subordinators, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and mark whichever side is in surplus. **But a coordinator and a subordinator the ASV writes together for one connective morpheme are one rendering of that morpheme, and neither word is a surplus.** Where the ASV recasts that connective's own clause as a subordinate one and writes the pair at that clause's left edge — *And when I looked* for וָאֶרְאֶה, *And when I see the blood* for וְרָאִיתִי, and likewise *and that* and *so that* — both English words belong to that connective's single unit, and the count above marks nothing `added` unless no conjunction stands in the clause at all. Contiguity is the test, exactly as in rule 30: what makes the Leviticus *if* above a surplus is that הִנֵּה's *behold* stands between it and the waw's *and*, so the *if* is written beside those renderings rather than as part of one connective. **Read the connective that is there and not its lemma.** A disjunctive אוֹ whose clause the ASV recasts the same way takes the pair on the same terms as a waw — `אוֹ־עָבַר עָלָיו רוּחַ־קִנְאָה` → ***or if*** *the spirit of jealousy come upon him* is one unit on the אוֹ, headed on *or* — since what licenses the pair is the one connective the ASV has rendered by it and not the lemma, exactly as rule 14 reads אוֹ and a waw alike where one connective is written in two English words. But where a morpheme of its own stands in the clause for the subordinator, that morpheme takes it and there is no pair to place: `אוֹ אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲבֹר עָלָיו` → *or* ***when*** *the spirit of jealousy cometh upon a man* gives *or* to the אוֹ and *when* to the אֲשֶׁר, a present morpheme taking its English before a fused reading does. Head such a unit on the coordinator, which is what the connective itself is; the corpus aligns a waw to *and when* in twenty-seven units, to *so that* in thirty-eight and to *and that* in eight, heading eleven of the *and when* units on *when* instead, so name that competing reading in the note under rule 8. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it, and the absence of one is not evidence against it, by rule 7. **And a subordinator the ASV writes a second time for a clause coordinated under one the Hebrew has already written is that morpheme's own repeated realization, not a surplus.** Where a single אֲשֶׁר or כִּי governs coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites its *that* at the head of a later one, every occurrence belongs to that morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit under rule 25, exactly as a distributed `מִן` takes both of its *from*s there and a paraphrased suffix takes both of its pronouns under rule 18; head on the first, and mark nothing `added`. `לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יִגְבְּהוּ ... וְלֹא־יִתְּנוּ ... וְלֹא־יַעַמְדוּ` → *to the end* ***that*** *none ... exalt themselves ..., neither set their top ..., nor* ***that*** *their mighty ones stand up* gives both *that*s to the one אֲשֶׁר, the waws keeping only the *neither* and *nor* they are fused into. So read whether the later clause is coordinated under an earlier subordinator's scope before counting: what the count governs is a subordinator standing over a clause no written subordinator reaches, as the Leviticus protasis above has no conjunction in it at all. **And a word that belongs to a formula's own fixed English rendering is not a subordinator supplied for the clause: it belongs to the morpheme the formula rests on.** The oath חַי־אָנִי is written *As I live*, and the *As* is what English spends on the adverbial force of that predicate adjective, exactly as rule 20 takes the copula from the construction and rule 30 takes the pronouns of נָא's *I beseech thee* from the particle's one idiomatic rendering: the adjective takes *As … live* in one unit, discontinuous around the pronoun under rule 25 and headed on *live*, while an explicit אָנִי or אֲנִי takes only its own *I*. The corpus reads the formula this way in six chapters and never marks the *As* `added`. So before counting an English subordinator as a surplus, read whether it is one the formula always writes; the count above governs a word the ASV has supplied for the clause, not a word the formula's rendering contains.
amendments.why: NUM.5.14 and NUM.5.27 are the same construction — one conjunction morpheme opening a clause the ASV recasts as subordinate, with a coordinator and a subordinator written contiguously at its left edge — and the chapter analysed them two ways because rule 55's pair clause said *one waw* and the morpheme at 5.14 is אוֹ. Rule 14 already states, for the adjacent case of one connective written in two English words, that what licenses the pair is the connective the ASV has rendered by it and not the lemma, so the restriction to a waw was an artefact of the case the rule had met rather than a qualification. The replacement widens the pair clause to any connective morpheme, adds the אוֹ example, and adds the limit NUM.5.30 supplies, where a written אֲשֶׁר takes the subordinator and nothing is fused. Everything else in the rule, including the waw-only corpus counts, the contiguity test, the repeated-subordinator paragraph and the חַי־אָנִי paragraph, is reproduced unchanged.

amendments.rule: Read `בֵּין X וּבֵין Y` by the connective the ASV actually writes. Where it is recast as *X from Y*, the second `בֵּין` carries *from*, while the first `בֵּין` and its waw are `unrepresented`. Where the ASV preserves *between X and Y*, the first `בֵּין` takes *between*, the waw takes *and*, and the repeated second `בֵּין` is `unrepresented`. Do not transfer the *and* to the repeated preposition: the waw is the morpheme that licenses it. **A verse may write more than one such pair, and the count runs pair by pair.** Where the ASV writes a *between* for each pair — `בֵּין הַקֹּדֶשׁ וּבֵין הַחֹל וּבֵין הַטָּמֵא וּבֵין הַטָּהוֹר` → *between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean* — each written *between* belongs to the `בֵּין` that opens the pair it stands before, only the `בֵּין` repeated inside a pair is `unrepresented`, and every waw keeps the *and* written for it. Do not read *the repeated second `בֵּין`* above as every `בֵּין` after the first in the phrase: count the ASV's *between*s against the pairs and read which pair each opens, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **Hebrew also writes the second member with `לְ` in place of a repeated `בֵּין`, and the same reading follows the morpheme that is actually there.** In `בֵּין X לְ Y` → *between X and Y* the `בֵּין` takes *between* and the `לְ` takes the *and*, exactly as the waw does above, because the `לְ` is what stands where the connective stands and no waw is present to claim it: `בֵּין שֶׂה לָשֶׂה` → *between sheep and sheep* is the shape. Do not mark such a `לְ` `unrepresented` in order to leave the *and* `added`, and do not reach for rule 14's last sentence: that sentence governs a connective no morpheme answers to, and here one does. **Where the phrase runs on into further `לְ` members the ASV writes as bare coordinated nouns, only the `לְ` standing where the ASV writes its connective takes one.** `בֵּין שֶׂה לָשֶׂה לָאֵילִים וְלָעַתּוּדִים` → *between sheep and sheep, the rams and the he goats* gives *and* to the first `לְ`, leaves the two later ones `unrepresented` under rule 40, and gives the second written *and* to the waw. Count the phrase's connective morphemes against the ASV's connectives and read which pair of members each stands between, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **A `מִן … עַד` range is read on the same terms, by the morpheme that stands where the ASV's connective stands.** Where the Hebrew writes the second endpoint with a waw, that waw takes the *and* and the `עַד` is `unrepresented` under rule 40, which is the reading rule 14 gives `מֵעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה` → ***both*** *the birds of the heavens* ***and*** *the beasts*. Where no waw is written, the bare `עַד` is what stands where the connective stands and it takes the *and* the ASV has written, exactly as the `לְ` member does above: `מִזָּכָר עַד נְקֵבָה` → ***both*** *male* ***and*** *female* gives *both* to the `מִן` under rule 14 and *and* to the `עַד`. Do not read rule 14's example as leaving every `עַד` `unrepresented`: what goes unrepresented there is a `עַד` whose connective a waw has already answered for, and a `עַד` no waw stands beside is not that. The corpus aligns a `עַד` to *and* in eight units across four chapters, including the waw-less `מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה` of GEN.6.7 and GEN.7.23, and the opening `מִן` still takes the *both* in either case, as its own ten corpus units do.
amendments.why: NUM.5.3 writes מִזָּכָר עַד נְקֵבָה with no waw, and rule 14's only מִן … עַד example has one, so the verse pass had to decide whether the ASV's *and* was the עַד's or `added`. The evidence round settled it: מִן → *both* has 10 aligned units headed on *both*, and עַד → *and* has 8 aligned units in 4 chapters, two of them the waw-less מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה of GEN.6.7 and GEN.7.23, while the waw case behaves as rule 14 says (GEN.19.11 assigns *both* to the opening preposition and leaves the closing one unrepresented). The qualification belongs in rule 26 because that is the rule about reading a two-member range by the connective the ASV actually writes, and it already disposes of the parallel בֵּין X לְ Y; the added paragraph says in terms how rule 14's example is to be read, so the over-broad reading is closed off rather than left standing. Rule 26's existing text is reproduced unchanged.

conventions: Cognate accusative with מָעַל: where the ASV writes a single English word for the verb and its cognate noun — לִמְעֹל מַעַל → *so as to trespass* (5.6) — the verb takes that word and the noun is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, because the word is a rendering the verb owns outright rather than one no morpheme owns a part of. Where the ASV writes a word for each — וּמָעֲלָה בוֹ מָעַל → *commit a trespass* (5.12), וַתִּמְעֹל מַעַל → *have committed a trespass* (5.27) — rule 2 splits them and the noun takes its own English with the indefinite article. The competing reading is rule 30's fusion on the one-English-word condition, which fuses a verb with its object noun in הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים → *deny*; BSB represents the noun at 5.6 and so reads it that way. The chapter took rule 22 throughout.

Where a written אִישׁ and a coreferent pronominal suffix are rendered by one English possessive, the noun takes it and the suffix is `unrepresented` under rule 22: אִישׁ אֶת־קָדָשָׁיו → *every man's hallowed things* (5.10) and אִישׁ אִישׁ … אִשְׁתּוֹ → *any man's wife* (5.12) both put *man's* on the noun. The reverse division is defensible and is what BSB records; the chapter did not take it.

A coordinator and a subordinator the ASV writes together at the left edge of a clause it has recast as subordinate are one rendering of the single conjunction morpheme standing in that clause, whatever that morpheme is: a waw at 5.27 (וְהִשְׁקָהּ → *And when he hath made her drink*) and a disjunctive אוֹ at 5.14 (אוֹ־עָבַר → *or if the spirit of jealousy come upon him*), each headed on the coordinator. Where a morpheme of its own stands for the subordinator it takes it instead and nothing is fused, as אֲשֶׁר does for the *when* of 5.30.

amended.text: Read `בֵּין X וּבֵין Y` by the connective the ASV actually writes. Where it is recast as *X from Y*, the second `בֵּין` carries *from*, while the first `בֵּין` and its waw are `unrepresented`. Where the ASV preserves *between X and Y*, the first `בֵּין` takes *between*, the waw takes *and*, and the repeated second `בֵּין` is `unrepresented`. Do not transfer the *and* to the repeated preposition: the waw is the morpheme that licenses it. **A verse may write more than one such pair, and the count runs pair by pair.** Where the ASV writes a *between* for each pair — `בֵּין הַקֹּדֶשׁ וּבֵין הַחֹל וּבֵין הַטָּמֵא וּבֵין הַטָּהוֹר` → *between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean* — each written *between* belongs to the `בֵּין` that opens the pair it stands before, only the `בֵּין` repeated inside a pair is `unrepresented`, and every waw keeps the *and* written for it. Do not read *the repeated second `בֵּין`* above as every `בֵּין` after the first in the phrase: count the ASV's *between*s against the pairs and read which pair each opens, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **Hebrew also writes the second member with `לְ` in place of a repeated `בֵּין`, and the same reading follows the morpheme that is actually there.** In `בֵּין X לְ Y` → *between X and Y* the `בֵּין` takes *between* and the `לְ` takes the *and*, exactly as the waw does above, because the `לְ` is what stands where the connective stands and no waw is present to claim it: `בֵּין שֶׂה לָשֶׂה` → *between sheep and sheep* is the shape. Do not mark such a `לְ` `unrepresented` in order to leave the *and* `added`, and do not reach for rule 14's last sentence: that sentence governs a connective no morpheme answers to, and here one does. **Where the phrase runs on into further `לְ` members the ASV writes as bare coordinated nouns, only the `לְ` standing where the ASV writes its connective takes one.** `בֵּין שֶׂה לָשֶׂה לָאֵילִים וְלָעַתּוּדִים` → *between sheep and sheep, the rams and the he goats* gives *and* to the first `לְ`, leaves the two later ones `unrepresented` under rule 40, and gives the second written *and* to the waw. Count the phrase's connective morphemes against the ASV's connectives and read which pair of members each stands between, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **A `מִן … עַד` range is read on the same terms, by the morpheme that stands where the ASV's connective stands.** Where the Hebrew writes the second endpoint with a waw, that waw takes the *and* and the `עַד` is `unrepresented` under rule 40, which is the reading rule 14 gives `מֵעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה` → ***both*** *the birds of the heavens* ***and*** *the beasts*. Where no waw is written, the bare `עַד` is what stands where the connective stands and it takes the *and* the ASV has written, exactly as the `לְ` member does above: `מִזָּכָר עַד נְקֵבָה` → ***both*** *male* ***and*** *female* gives *both* to the `מִן` under rule 14 and *and* to the `עַד`. Do not read rule 14's example as leaving every `עַד` `unrepresented`: what goes unrepresented there is a `עַד` whose connective a waw has already answered for, and a `עַד` no waw stands beside is not that. The corpus aligns a `עַד` to *and* in eight units across four chapters, including the waw-less `מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה` of GEN.6.7 and GEN.7.23, and the opening `מִן` still takes the *both* in either case, as its own ten corpus units do.
amended.why: NUM.5.3 writes מִזָּכָר עַד נְקֵבָה with no waw, and rule 14's only מִן … עַד example has one, so the verse pass had to decide whether the ASV's *and* was the עַד's or `added`. The evidence round settled it: מִן → *both* has 10 aligned units headed on *both*, and עַד → *and* has 8 aligned units in 4 chapters, two of them the waw-less מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה of GEN.6.7 and GEN.7.23, while the waw case behaves as rule 14 says (GEN.19.11 assigns *both* to the opening preposition and leaves the closing one unrepresented). The qualification belongs in rule 26 because that is the rule about reading a two-member range by the connective the ASV actually writes, and it already disposes of the parallel בֵּין X לְ Y; the added paragraph says in terms how rule 14's example is to be read, so the over-broad reading is closed off rather than left standing. Rule 26's existing text is reproduced unchanged.

report: All three evidence requests were answered; nothing is left outstanding. I read all 51 candidate groups and, because the table is blind to `added` units, the whole dump end to end for the chapter's 12 supplied-English units.

One real split, patched. A coordinator and a subordinator written together at a recast clause's left edge: NUM.5.27 gives *And when* whole to the waw as one rendering under rule 55's pair clause, while NUM.5.14 gave *or* to the אוֹ and marked *if* `added`. Nothing in the source licenses the difference except the connective's lemma, and rule 14 says the lemma is not what licenses such a pair. NUM.5.14 now reads *or if* as one unit on אוֹ, headed on *or*. NUM.5.27 and NUM.5.30 (where a written אֲשֶׁר takes the *when*, so the count is balanced) are already right and are untouched.

NUM.5.3's מִזָּכָר עַד נְקֵבָה → *both … and* is confirmed by the evidence round and left standing: מִן → *both* has 10 aligned corpus units headed on *both*, and עַד → *and* has 8 units across 4 chapters, including the waw-less מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה of GEN.6.7 and GEN.7.23. Rule 14's וְעַד example is the waw case, where the waw answers for the connective, and it does not reach a bare עַד. Promoted as an amendment to rule 26 so the next chapter does not have to re-derive it.

Near-misses checked and left as they stand: the demonstrative/article count in 5.6, 5.19, 5.22, 5.23, 5.30 and 5.31 (the demonstrative morpheme takes the determiner and both articles go unrepresented, which is rule 29's own הֶעָרִים הָאֵלֶּה reading together with rule 41's "only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner"); אֵת taking *of*, *with*, *for* or *as* where the English verb reaches its object through a preposition and unrepresented elsewhere (5.7, 5.13, 5.14, 5.19, 5.26, 5.30 — 5.8 and 5.20 differ because no marker stands on the object there, exactly as rules 16 and 44 divide them); the whole לְ set; מִן as *out of* in 5.2 and 5.25 against the verb's own particle *out* in 5.3 and 5.4, where the ASV also writes *without* for מִחוּץ; and the supplied object pronouns and coordinators marked `added` in 5.7, 5.17, 5.22, 5.23, 5.24, 5.26 and 5.27, which agree with each other and with the verses where an object morpheme or a waw is present.

BSB: no genuine error. Twelve of the thirteen disagreement groups are the documented convention differences — לֵאמֹר's preposition (rule 27), prepositions silenced by an ASV recasting (rule 40), object markers (rule 16), articles whose determiner a present demonstrative takes (rules 15, 29, 41), coreferent suffixes rendered once (rule 22), and 5.28's הִוא, for which the ASV's gapped clause writes no pronoun at all.

The one substantive BSB candidate is NUM.5.6 מַעַל, where the ASV writes one word for לִמְעֹל מַעַל and the chapter marks the cognate noun `unrepresented` under rule 22 while 5.12 and 5.27 give it *a trespass* because the ASV writes a second word there. I left it: the single *trespass* is a rendering the infinitive owns outright, which is an element the ASV has left unwritten rather than a fusion no morpheme owns a part of. The competing reading is real and is rule 30's הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים → *deny*, which fuses a verb with its object noun on the one-English-word condition; it is now named in the conventions log so a later chapter meets it. The corpus query neither settles nor contradicts this: 108 מַעַל units and not one `unrepresented`, but also not one where the ASV spends a single English word on a verb and its cognate noun.

Two amendments returned, no new rules. Rule 55 is widened from *one waw* to one connective morpheme, which is what carried the patch; rule 26 is widened to the מִן … עַד range, which is what the evidence round carried.
